title: Quoting and changing
hook: he kept adding to the Essays in the margins until he died

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Catholic doubter: Montaigne asked what do I know? and stayed in his church. Your line was faith and doubt. What question did you let sit beside what you trust? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-seven.

Open a secondhand book and sometimes there's a stranger in it: pencil in the margins, a word underlined, a question mark, a date, a small argument with the author. Tradition says Montaigne did something like that to his own book. Once the Essays were printed and out in the world, he kept adding to them: new sentences, new quotations, second thoughts that didn't erase the first ones. Today, a book that never quite stopped being written, and the man who said why.
screen: `PENCIL IN THE MARGINS.` → `HIS OWN PRINTED BOOK.` → `SECOND THOUGHTS, FIRST ONES KEPT.`

segments.voice: First, the rule he gave himself. In the essay Of vanity, Montaigne says it plainly: I add, but I don't correct. Once the book had gone out, he felt it belonged partly to its readers. And he wasn't sure his later self was wiser than his earlier one. Myself now and myself a while ago, he says, are indeed two. So the old self keeps its say, and the new self adds a note beside it. Second, the quoting. His pages are full of other people's words, many of them in Latin. In the essay Of books he explains. He makes others say what he can't say so well himself. Third, his trick. Sometimes, he admits, he leaves the author's name off on purpose. That way a critic who sneers at the line, thinking it's his, ends up flicking Plutarch on the nose, or burning his fingers insulting Seneca. Fourth, what this makes the book. Not a monument but a conversation, his voice and the old voices, his younger thoughts and his older ones, all left standing on the same page. Your life has old pages too: a letter, a journal, an opinion you held loudly. You don't have to tear them out. You can write beside them.
screen: `I ADD, BUT I DON'T CORRECT.` · `MYSELF NOW AND THEN ARE TWO.` · `OTHERS SAY IT BETTER.` · `A NOTE BESIDE THE OLD PAGE.` · then, large: `KEEP ADDING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: add a note to an old page. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind something you once said, wrote or firmly believed, a few years back. Don't judge that younger self. Let them have their say first. Then, quietly, add one line beside it, the way Montaigne added to his own pages. Not a correction. Just what you'd add now. If you have paper nearby, you can write it down after the bell. The bell holds the time.
Quoting and changing. Montaigne filled his book with other people's words and kept adding his own, without crossing out what he'd said before. Today's word.
Your line: keep adding. Today, find one old note, message or page of yours, and add a line to it instead of deleting it. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Montaigne says in the essay Of vanity that he adds to his book but does not correct it, and in Of books that he borrows other writers' words to say what he cannot say as well.

fork.setup: your book is printed and out in the world. you've changed your mind about a page. what does Montaigne do?
options: cross it out and rewrite it.
add a new thought beside it and leave the old one standing.
fork.reveal: I add, but I don't correct. the old self keeps its say; the new self writes beside it.

trapdoor: what you thought: quoting other writers is showing off.
what it means: Montaigne borrowed others' words to say what he couldn't say as well, and kept adding his own without erasing.

what a scholar hears: his later additions sit beside earlier text rather than replacing it, so readers can watch his thinking change on the same page; tradition says he was still adding near the end of his life.

sources.ref: Essays 3.9, Of vanity (he adds but does not correct; himself now and himself a while ago are two)

notes: Montaigne paraphrased throughout; 'I add, but I don't correct' and 'myself now and myself a while ago are indeed two' are paraphrases of 3.9, not quotations from a listed translation.
